# Module map — Credit risk and underwriting ML that survives an audit

A module is one lesson directory in the standard layout (`meta.yaml`, `lesson.py`,
`solutions/`, `tests/`, `claims.yaml`). Every module is tier `cpu8` — 8 GiB, 2 vCPU, no GPU, no
network, under ten minutes — and each section states the budget its `meta.yaml` declares, or will
declare. Every module is Python, numpy and matplotlib only, and every one runs on data generated
in the notebook from a fixed seed. Modules 1 to 3 are built; the others are
specified here and have no directory.

## Module 1 — PD modelling with vintages and macro overlays

**Lesson:** `lessons/P05-L01-pd-vintages-and-macro/` · tier `cpu8` · budget 120 s · prerequisite
`T00-L01-the-8gb-track`.

A probability of default with a term structure is what both CECL and IFRS 9 need: the allowance is
measured over the life of the loan, and IFRS 9 also asks for the 12-month part of it (sources in
`claims.yaml`, as read on 29 September 2026). This module builds that PD from monthly loan performance by origination cohort,
and then does what a validator does with it.

**The catalog's lab, and what changed.** The catalog asks the student to load Fannie Mae loan
performance data with a scripted loader and back-test through the 2020 shock. The Fannie Mae data
page refused automated access, so its terms could not be verified, and the Freddie Mac dataset
needs registration and is free only for non-commercial and research use. Neither belongs on a
required path of a lesson that must open in an empty directory. The lesson instead simulates a
consumer loan book from a fixed seed with a planted unemployment-like macro path, a planted
recession that arrives after the model is built, and planted vintage quality that drifts. A planted
truth lets the back-test be marked right or wrong. Freddie Mac is offered as an optional exercise
for a student who registers.

**The lab.** The student implements ten functions in numpy:

1. `risk_table()` — loans at risk and defaults by vintage and month on book, in which a censored
   loan is at risk for every month it was watched and is never a default.
2. `vintage_curves()` — cumulative default rate by vintage, by the product limit, `nan` where the
   data stop rather than carried forward.
3. `oot_masks()` — an out-of-time split by vintage with a calendar cut, so that a model built at a
   date sees nothing after it.
4. `design_matrix()` — one intercept per month on book plus a macro covariate, with no separate
   constant.
5. `binomial_nll_grad()` — the grouped logistic loss and its gradient, stable for large linear
   predictors.
6. `gradient_check()` — central differences, reporting the worst relative error.
7. `fit_newton()` — Newton's method with a tiny ridge, stopped on the Newton decrement.
8. `actual_vs_expected()` — calibration by any grouping, on observed cells only.
9. `term_structure()` — cumulative PD under a macro scenario, read by calendar month rather than
   by age.
10. `expected_credit_loss()` — 12-month and lifetime loss from a term structure, weighted by the
    marginal PD.

**What the student measures.** Nothing here is asserted in prose; the notebook prints each of
these. The naive default rate against the product-limit rate for the young vintages, which have
not been watched long enough to have one. The actual-over-expected ratio of the model on each test
vintage, through a recession the model was never shown, next to the hidden vintage quality the
generator planted. The same fitted model as a point-in-time and a through-the-cycle PD, with the
caveat that a through-the-cycle average taken over a quiet window is not through any cycle. And
four protocols that can flatter the back-test, each scored beside the out-of-time number: a random
split, training months after the model's date, scoring with the macro that actually happened, and
a feature built from the outcomes. Then the same back-test on six more books drawn from the same
generator, because one book is one draw: the student sees which numbers move from draw to draw
and which do not.

**What it is graded on.** Partial credit throughout. Among the cases it grades: censored loans
are never dropped and never defaults; the observed edge of every vintage curve is exact for every
data cut-off; the macro path is read by calendar month; a cumulative PD never falls as the horizon
grows; and a gradient that is wrong in one coordinate of forty is flagged. The rubric was
mutation-tested against plausible-wrong implementations, and against correct ones written
differently, which still score full marks.

## Module 2 — Reject inference and selection bias

**Lesson:** `lessons/P05-L02-reject-inference/` · tier `cpu8` · budget 120 s · prerequisites
`T00-L01-the-8gb-track`, `P04-L01-validation-suite` and `P05-L01-pd-vintages-and-macro`.

A lender learns outcomes only for the applicants it approved. A scorecard fitted on approvals is
then used to score everyone, including the people the old policy declined.

**The catalog's lab, and what changes.** The catalog imposes an approve/decline policy on the Bank
Account Fraud data. That suite is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 per its datasheet, so no extract can be
committed here, and it is an account-opening fraud dataset rather than a credit one. The lab
instead generates an applicant population in which every applicant has a latent outcome, so the
counterfactual the real world hides is known.

**The lab.** Impose an approval policy with a known cut-off. Fit a scorecard on the approvals
only and on the full population, and measure how much rank ordering and calibration degrade. Then
implement the remedies (augmentation by weighting, parcelling, and a bounds analysis) and score
each against the truth. The student measures how the degradation changes with the severity of the
old policy and with how strongly the old policy depended on a variable the new model cannot see.
In the lesson's world the main damage is to calibration, not ranking: ranking barely moves except
under the strictest policies, and a holdout drawn from approvals alone can look calibrated while
understating how well the scorecard ranks everyone who applied.

## Module 3 — Scorecards versus boosting, with monotonicity

**Lesson:** `lessons/P05-L03-scorecard-versus-boosting/` · tier `cpu8` · budget 300 s · prerequisites
`T00-L01-the-8gb-track`, `P04-L07-challenger-from-scratch` and `P05-L01-pd-vintages-and-macro`.

**The catalog's lab, and what changes.** The catalog compares a weight-of-evidence scorecard with
LightGBM under monotone constraints. This environment has neither optbinning nor LightGBM, so the
lesson carries the scorecard in from `P04-L07` as given code and the student builds the boosted
challenger: a histogram split search that refuses splits which break a stated monotone direction,
trees that hand bounds down after every constrained split, and a boosting loop whose size is chosen
on out-of-time months.

**The lab.** On a generated application book with known monotone truths (risk falls with age of
account, rises with utilisation), the student compares the scorecard, an unconstrained booster, a
booster whose constraint is checked at each split alone and a booster whose bounds are handed down,
on discrimination and on stability, reporting the population stability index alongside the Gini.
As built, the lesson has seven exercises: the gradient and hessian of the logistic loss, the
regularised leaf weight clipped into inherited bounds, the constrained split search, tree growth
with bounds, the boosting loop, the out-of-time loss curve that picks the number of trees, and a
monotonicity test over every reference application on a grid made of the model's own thresholds.
The student measures what a check at the split alone lets through, what the constraint costs in
development fit, what it buys in stability on shifted months, and how much of that is one draw,
over replicate books from the same generator. No threshold for a population stability index is
adopted.

## Module 4 — Adverse action and reason codes *(specified)*

**Status: specified.** python · tier `cpu8` · budget 120 s.

Regulation B requires the statement of reasons for an adverse action to be specific, and says that
a bare failure to reach a qualifying score is not enough. CFPB Circular 2022-03 applied that to
complex algorithms and was withdrawn from 12 May 2025; the regulation's text, which this module
builds against, did not change (sources in `claims.yaml`, as read on 29 September 2026).

**The catalog's lab, and what changes.** The catalog generates reason codes from SHAP values. The
SHAP library is not available, so the student computes exact Shapley values for a small model by
enumeration and checks them against the additivity property.

**The lab.** Generate Regulation B-style reason codes from the attributions of a declined
applicant, then write up, with counterexamples the lab constructs, where a ranking of attributions
is not a defensible reason: two correlated features that split credit, an attribution that
depends on the reference population chosen, and a reason that the applicant could not act on. The
student measures how often the top reason changes when only the reference population changes.

## Module 5 — Disparity testing without protected attributes *(specified)*

**Status: specified.** python · tier `cpu8` · budget 180 s.

Lenders are often not allowed to collect the attribute they are asked to test for, so fair lending
analysis uses a proxy. Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding, the method a 2014 CFPB paper describes,
combines geography- and surname-based information into a single probability (source in
`claims.yaml`).

**The catalog's lab, and what changes.** The catalog applies BISG-style proxies to HMDA loan-level
data. HMDA data are public, but the loan-level files and the Census surname and geography tables
are large downloads, and a required path may not fetch them. The lab generates a population with a
planted group, planted surname and geography tables, and a planted disparity in approval and
pricing. HMDA is an optional extension.

**The lab.** Implement the Bayesian update, then compute approval and pricing disparities by the
proxy-weighted group with bootstrap confidence intervals. The student measures how far the proxy
attenuates a true disparity, how the interval widens with proxy uncertainty, and when a disparity
that is real is indistinguishable from none.

## Module 6 — Thin-file and cash-flow underwriting *(specified)*

**Status: specified.** python · tier `cpu8` · budget 180 s.

**The catalog's lab, and what changes.** The catalog generates loan origination and repayment
histories in Apache Fineract in Docker. Fineract is open source under the Apache License 2.0
(source in `claims.yaml`), but it needs a container runtime and a service, which no notebook
service on the required path can assume. The lab generates account transaction histories in the
notebook.

**The lab.** Engineer cash-flow features (income regularity, buffer, volatility, obligation
ratios) from generated transaction histories and compare them with bureau-style features on
thin-file and thick-file applicants. The student measures the lift the cash-flow features give
on each population, and what the model does when a feature that only exists for some applicants is
missing for others.

## Module 7 — Monitoring and the model risk file *(specified)*

**Status: specified.** python · tier `cpu8` · budget 180 s.

**The catalog's lab, and what changes.** The catalog ships a dashboard built with Evidently plus a
validation report. Evidently is not available; the student builds the drift, override and outcome
statistics themselves and renders the dashboard with matplotlib.

**The lab.** Monitor a generated live portfolio for population drift, override rate and outcomes
by vintage, with thresholds whose false-alarm rate the student measures rather than adopts. Then
generate a validation report from the results, mapped section by section to SR 26-2. The
guidance is organised in seven parts: introduction, purpose and scope, overview, development and
use, validation and monitoring, governance and controls, and vendor and other third-party
products (source in `claims.yaml`). A gate fails the report if a figure in it cannot be traced to
a computed result.

## Module 8 — Capstone: a consumer-credit decisioning repo *(specified)*

**Status: specified.** python · tier `cpu8` · budget 300 s.

The catalog's capstone: a consumer-credit decisioning repository with a scorecard and a machine
learning challenger, an adverse-action notice generator, a proxy-based disparity test, a
monitoring dashboard and a validation report mapped section by section to SR 26-2, built so that
an employer can read the report in ten minutes and see whether the candidate understands evidence,
not just estimators.

**What changes.** The catalog builds it on Fannie Mae data and HMDA. Here it is built on the
generated book from the earlier modules, so that it runs on the required path; a student who has
registered for the Freddie Mac dataset may substitute it, and must not commit it. The capstone is
graded on whether every figure in the report traces to a computed result, whether the out-of-time
back-test is cut before the model runs, and whether each reason code survives the counterexamples
of module 4.

---

## What is deliberately not here

- **No policy templates and no committee terms of reference.** They are useful and they are not
  analytics.
- **No claim about any lender's practice.** Every module runs on generated data and says so.
- **No real credit data committed to this repository.** The terms of the datasets the catalog
  names are recorded in the README, and none of them permits it or could be verified as permitting
  it.
- **No LGD or exposure-at-default module.** Module 1 uses an assumed loss given default and
  exposure profile, labelled as assumptions. Estimating them is a real gap in this map and the
  most likely addition.
